Protects against overfitting / false certainty / mis-calibration / external bias / naive extrapolation / ignoring design / ignoring residuals.
rationale_evidence.statement: Reads the seven pillars as an 'anti-reasoner' -- each pillar mapped to a protective function (against overfitting, false certainty, mis-calibration, external bias, naive extrapolation, ignoring design, ignoring residuals) -- concluding the pillars form a theory of extracting signal from noise and managing uncertainty, not a theory of knowledge, and that a Knowledge Kernel needs an analogous operation set to avoid treating data as self-evident truth.

rationale_evidence.anchor: DDD treats aggregates as identity holders. But Stigler's aggregation is about discarding identity to reveal signal. ... DDD treats residuals as error. But Stigler shows that residuals are often the source of discovery.
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten questions framed as blind spots of conventional DDD analysis relative to Stigler's pillars (identity-vs-discarded-identity in aggregates, equal-value-vs-diminishing-returns data, probability-as-truth-vs-calibration, generation-independent-vs-design-dependent data, residuals-as-error-vs-signal, symmetric-vs-directional relationships, valid-vs-trap extrapolation, root-n diminishing value, optional-vs-inference-creating randomization, and always-better-vs-sometimes-discard 'more data').

rationale_evidence.anchor: These are not questions about missing capabilities. They are questions about the assumptions the Kernel makes about how information is extracted, calibrated, and validated from data.
rationale_evidence.statement: Final ten-question architect checklist (raw-vs-aggregated data, diminishing marginal value, probability-as-truth-vs-calibration, internal-vs-external validity standards, symmetric-vs-directional relationships, generation-process awareness, residual-as-error-vs-signal, proportional-extrapolation risk, marginal-contribution weighting, first-class data reduction), explicitly framed as questions about the Kernel's assumptions rather than about missing capabilities.
